pyramide.signal: In the Plateau business district, a stepped concrete pyramid like a spaceship, with huge murals on its walls and almost nothing inside.
pyramide.what: A 15-storey Brutalist building designed by the Italian architect Rinaldo Olivieri, begun in 1968 and finished in 1973, one of Plateau's first high-rises. The idea was to bring the bustle of an African market into a city building.
pyramide.why: It embodies the optimism of the 'Ivorian miracle': open volumes for ventilation and precast panels for shade, modernism designed for the tropics. High maintenance costs and inefficient space later left it largely abandoned.
pyramide.meaning: It is one of the most cited buildings of 'African modernism'. In 2023 the Ministry of Culture's 'Pyramid 2023' project invited artists to paint its façades, and in 2026 an international architecture competition sought ideas to revive it. Its fate mirrors how Abidjan deals with its own past.
pyramide.use: Stand at its foot with guests who like architecture and tell the three stages, miracle, abandonment and artistic revival. It is a complete city story.
pyramide.bridge: Compare the preservation debates over Japanese Metabolist buildings (such as the Nakagin Capsule Tower), or the arguments before and after Taipei's Zhonghua Market was demolished.
pyramide.where: Plateau; easy to pair with St Paul's Cathedral and the Museum of Civilisations on the same day.

ivoire.signal: A 25-storey white tower on the lagoon in Cocody, where national conferences, launches and weddings all take place.
ivoire.what: Designed by the Israeli architect Moshe Mayer and opened in 1963, it once had an ice rink, a cinema and a conference centre. It is now run by Sofitel and has a casino; a new renovation was announced in September 2026.
ivoire.why: It was Houphouët-Boigny's showcase of the 'Ivorian miracle' to the world. Soon after it opened, The New York Times called it perhaps the most dazzling hotel in Africa. It rose and fell through the crisis years and reopened under the Sofitel brand in 2014.
ivoire.meaning: It is still the nation's social stage: MASA and FEMUA launches, Art Week partnerships and foreign delegations all pass through.
ivoire.use: When hosting senior guests, a drink here while talking about its era makes better conversation than any new hotel.
ivoire.bridge: Like Taipei's Grand Hotel: the national showpiece of an era.

basilica.nameZh: Basilica of Our Lady of Peace, Yamoussoukro
basilica.signal: On the grassland of a small town, a domed church almost the size of St Peter's in Rome suddenly appears.
basilica.what: Built by Houphouët-Boigny in his home town of Yamoussoukro and modelled on St Peter's, it was constructed in 1985–1989 and consecrated by Pope John Paul II on 10 September 1990. It is often listed among the largest churches in the world. Visits are paid and guided.
basilica.why: It was the founding father's personal legacy project and part of 'bringing the capital home'. It was built during an economic crisis, and its cost was hotly debated abroad.
basilica.meaning: It stands for the president's ambition, the place of Catholicism in the south, and the politics of grand projects.
basilica.use: A must on any visit to Yamoussoukro. Talk about its scale, stained glass and history, but when the cost comes up, be mindful of how your hosts feel about the founding father.
basilica.bridge: Compare monuments that leaders have built in their home towns around the world, or St Peter's itself.
basilica.where: Yamoussoukro; combine with the crocodile lake at the presidential palace.

mosques.nameZh: Sudanese-style mud mosques of the north
mosques.signal: A low, solid, earth-coloured mosque with a pyramid-shaped minaret and wooden stakes sticking out of its walls like a hedgehog.
mosques.what: Eight Sudanese-style mud mosques in the north, at Tengréla, Kouto, Sorobango, Samatiguila, Nambira, Kong, Kaouara and elsewhere, were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2021. The protruding stakes are both structure and scaffolding for the yearly re-plastering.
mosques.why: The style began in Djenné, Mali, and was carried south along the trade routes by Mandé merchants seeking kola nuts and gold, a testament to the blending of Senufo and Malinké cultures. In the 1920s there were nearly 300 such mosques; only about 20 remain.
mosques.meaning: They show that northern Côte d'Ivoire is part of Saharan civilisation, and remind people that the country is more than its coast and cocoa.
mosques.use: A good topic for getting closer to friends from the north. For Asian guests, 'Africa has its own tradition of Islamic architecture' breaks stereotypes.
mosques.bridge: Compare earthen architecture along the Silk Road, or the Japanese practice of periodic rebuilding at Ise, where renewal keeps a building alive.
mosques.where: Kong, Kouto, Tengréla and other northern towns; usually combined with a trip to Korhogo.

bassam.signal: In a seaside town, rows of colonial buildings with verandas and wooden balconies; some have collapsed under tree roots, others have become galleries and cafés.
bassam.what: Côte d'Ivoire's first colonial capital, about an hour's drive away. Its historic quarter was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2012. It is also the seat of the N'zima kingdom.
bassam.why: A yellow fever epidemic drove the government out in 1900, and trade later moved to Abidjan's deep-water port, so the colonial buildings were 'frozen' in time.
bassam.meaning: It holds both colonial history and N'zima royal tradition, a place where two worlds exist side by side. Every year at Abissa the whole town comes alive.
bassam.use: The best half-day trip for guests. Open with: 'This was once the capital; a yellow fever epidemic stopped it in 1900.' End with grilled fish by the sea.
bassam.bridge: Like Anping in Tainan or Tamsui: port, colonial buildings and today's creative scene layered together.
bassam.where: Quartier France; the National Costume Museum; a craft market on the road towards Abidjan.

stpaul.signal: A strikingly shaped church on the Plateau lagoon front: a huge tilted cross held by rows of cables, like a figure with arms outstretched.
stpaul.what: A modernist cathedral designed by the Italian architect Aldo Spirito, begun in 1980 and consecrated by Pope John Paul II in August 1985. Its stained glass places African people, plants and animals alongside Bible stories.
stpaul.why: Like La Pyramide, it is an attempt to 'speak Africa in modern architecture', and it is a spiritual landmark for the Catholic community of the south.
stpaul.meaning: It is one of the most recognisable buildings on Abidjan's skyline, visible from across the lagoon. During the 2011 crisis about 1,800 people sheltered here.
stpaul.use: Talk about architecture rather than faith: the symbolism of the form and the African imagery in the stained glass.
stpaul.bridge: Compare Luce Memorial Chapel at Tunghai University in Taiwan: both reinterpret religious space with modern structure.

mcci.nameZh: Museum of Civilisations of Côte d'Ivoire
mcci.signal: An unassuming colonial building in Plateau, holding masks, statues, gold weights and thrones from every group in the country.
mcci.what: The national museum, founded in 1942 as the colonial government's crafts centre and renamed the Museum of Civilisations in 1994. A major renovation began in 2024 with a budget of about 2.2 billion CFA francs.
mcci.why: If you want to see objects from all four cultural worlds in one place, this is it.
mcci.meaning: It also connects to the global debate on restitution: whether Ivorian objects in European museums should come home is a live issue.
mcci.use: The first stop with Asian guests. Build the 'base map' here, then visit galleries for contemporary art, and guests will see the link between tradition and today.
mcci.bridge: Compare the political meaning of the National Palace Museum's collection, and the global debate on returning cultural objects.
mcci.where: Plateau; check opening status during the renovation.

fakhoury.signal: A white, minimalist space in Cocody with installation and framing of international standard; collectors, diplomats and artists at the openings.
fakhoury.what: A contemporary art gallery opened in Abidjan in 2012, now with spaces in Abidjan, Dakar and Paris, and a regular at international fairs such as 1-54 and Art Basel Miami Beach.
fakhoury.why: It opened just as the 2011 crisis ended, betting that Abidjan would again become a West African art centre, and it did help build a local collectors' market.
fakhoury.meaning: It is a key gateway linking local artists to international price levels; when Ouattara Watts showed here in 2026, the First Lady received him personally.
fakhoury.use: Asking 'Which fairs has this artist shown at?' sounds more knowing than asking the price. Openings are a good place to meet Abidjan's elite.
fakhoury.bridge: Like a top Taipei gallery: started locally, building artists' prices through international fairs.

donwahi.signal: A striking high red wall in Cocody, behind it three minimalist villas with exhibition rooms, a library and a lounge.
donwahi.what: A non-profit contemporary art foundation founded in 2008 in memory of former National Assembly president Charles Bauza Donwahi, now led by Illa Ginette Donwahi.
donwahi.why: It was among the first art venues to reopen after the crisis, has shown the Sindika Dokolo collection, and gave the Spanish painter Antoni Clavé his first exhibition in Africa.
donwahi.meaning: A typical case of family money supporting a public art platform, and a social hub of Abidjan's art world.
donwahi.use: Its president often makes the point that Picasso's Cubism owed much to West African masks. Use it to open a conversation about Africa's influence on European modern art. The lounge is a good place to sit with guests.
donwahi.bridge: Like corporate or family foundation museums in Asia.

guirandou.signal: Next to the Goethe-Institut, a gallery converted from a villa with a pool; the summer shows feature young artists you have never heard of.
guirandou.what: Art historian Simone Guirandou-N'Diaye founded Arts Pluriels in 1991, one of the country's first galleries; in 2015 she and her daughter Gazelle opened this new space. The name combines Gazelle's parents' names, Louis and Simone.
guirandou.why: Two generations, mother and daughter, span thirty years of Abidjan's gallery scene, from traditional art to emerging contemporary artists.
guirandou.meaning: Its 'Découvertes' summer show is an important window onto emerging West African artists.
guirandou.use: The story behind the gallery's name opens conversation more easily than the works do. Come here to buy artists while they are still affordable.
guirandou.bridge: Like an old Japanese gallery that the next generation turns towards contemporary art.
guirandou.where: Cocody Mermoz, next to the Goethe-Institut; open Tuesday to Saturday.

watts.signal: Large abstract paintings with numbers, symbols, cosmic diagrams and fabric collage, in intense, ritual colours.
watts.what: Born in Abidjan in 1957, he met Jean-Michel Basquiat in Paris and moved to New York. He is one of Côte d'Ivoire's most internationally established living painters.
watts.why: His work brings together West African symbols, African spiritual beliefs and New York abstraction, a pioneer of the 'global African artist'.
watts.meaning: In 2026 his solo show for the first time gathered works on paper he made in Côte d'Ivoire, and the First Lady received him personally, a sign that the state treats international artists as soft power.
watts.use: His friendship with Basquiat gives everyone a way in. Then ask where the symbols in his paintings come from and let the gallery staff or collectors tell the story. Asking good questions is what insiders do.
watts.bridge: Like Zao Wou-Ki for the Chinese-speaking world: famous in a Western art capital, always carrying the worldview of home in his painting.

aboudia.signal: Childlike, graffiti-style figures with big eyes, collaged newspaper and comics, crowded and full of energy.
aboudia.what: An Abidjan painter whose style comes from street graffiti and Nouchi culture; works he made in a basement during the 2011 crisis brought him international fame.
aboudia.why: He put the crisis years and the viewpoint of street children onto canvas, recording a city's most chaotic moment.
aboudia.meaning: He is the most visible of a new generation of Ivorian artists on the market, and proof that crisis can become cultural capital.
aboudia.use: He is often compared with Basquiat. Discussing whether the comparison is fair is far more tasteful than simply saying they look alike.
aboudia.bridge: Compare Asian street and pop art, which also grew from the visual language of the city's streets.
aboudia.where: Rotonde des Arts; African contemporary art sales at international auction houses.

artweek.signal: For one week every April, galleries, foundations and art centres across the city open shows and hold talks at the same time, ending in Grand-Bassam.
artweek.what: Founded by Yacouba Konaté, philosophy professor and director of the Rotonde des Arts. The first edition was held during the 2024 Africa Cup of Nations; 14 galleries took part in 2025, and the third edition ran from 7 to 11 April 2026.
artweek.why: Abidjan wants to turn its post-crisis economic strength into status as a cultural centre, competing with Dakar to be West Africa's art capital.
artweek.meaning: Senegal's art world has a joke: 'Abidjan has the money, but Dakar has the taste.' Art Week is Abidjan's reply.
artweek.use: Use the joke to open a conversation about the rivalry between the two cities and you will immediately sound like an insider. Art Week is the best time to meet the whole city's art scene in one week.
artweek.bridge: Like Art Week in Taipei or Hong Kong: one week that links up all the art venues in a city.

dakart.signal: Dakar in November and December: exhibitions everywhere at once, in the old Palais de Justice, the Museum of Black Civilisations and venues large and small across the city, divided into the official IN and the independent OFF.
dakart.what: Conceived in 1989 and first held in 1990, it is Africa's longest-running major contemporary art biennale. The 16th edition runs from 19 November to 19 December 2026, with artistic director Morad Montazami and the theme '(Anti)fragilité', the art of repair.
dakart.why: Since Senegal's first president, the poet Senghor, the country has treated culture as central to national identity, and the biennale continues that line.
dakart.meaning: It is the most important gathering of Africa's art world, and the confidence behind the line 'Dakar has the taste'.
dakart.use: Knowing the difference between IN and OFF, and that the 2024 edition was postponed by six months because of politics, marks you as an insider.
dakart.bridge: Africa's Venice Biennale; this year Dak'Art opens three days before the Venice Biennale closes.
dakart.where: Dakar: Museum of Black Civilisations, the old Palais de Justice, the IFAN museum and more.

masa.nameZh: MASA, the African performing arts market
masa.signal: In April of even years, the area around the Palais de la Culture in Treichville fills with dancers, theatre companies and storytellers from many countries, and programme buyers in suits.
masa.what: A pan-African performing arts event held every two years since 1993, at once a marketplace, a professional forum and a festival. The 14th edition ran from 11 to 18 April 2026, with entries from 51 countries.
masa.why: What African performing companies lack is not talent but buyers and touring networks. MASA was designed to bring the world's programme buyers to one place.
masa.meaning: It shows Côte d'Ivoire wants to be the market for Africa's cultural industries, not just a festival host. The next edition is in 2028.
masa.use: Sum up the difference in one line: 'MASA is not just a festival, it's a market.' For anyone wanting to bring African performances to Asia, this is the most important week.
masa.bridge: Like the Edinburgh Fringe combined with a performing arts market, with a layer of cultural diplomacy on top.

femua.nameZh: FEMUA, the Anoumabo urban music festival
femua.signal: In spring, a big stage goes up in an unassuming old neighbourhood of Marcory, and African stars perform here, mostly for free.
femua.what: Founded in 2008 by A'Salfo, lead singer of Magic System, in Anoumabo, where he grew up; proceeds go to local schools and health care. The 18th edition in 2026 featured Youssou N'Dour and Fatoumata Diawara.
femua.why: Anoumabo was an Ebrié village that lost its land as the city expanded. The festival made the community visible again.
femua.meaning: It is a model of stars giving back to their community, and a showcase of Ivorian pop culture to the whole continent.
femua.use: The point is not the line-up but 'a music festival that builds schools'. That is what locals are proudest of.
femua.bridge: Like a star going home to stage a festival with a charitable foundation.
femua.where: Every spring, around Anoumabo in Marcory.

abissa.signal: Late October to early November, the streets of Grand-Bassam fill with drums; men dress as women and women as men; people openly criticise the king and officials.
abissa.what: The traditional New Year festival of the N'zima Kotoko. It begins when the sacred drum Edo N'Gbolé is brought out of the forest and handed to the king, and lasts about two weeks. Its core values are forgiveness, reconciliation and unity.
abissa.why: During the festival anyone may speak freely, including about the king and officials, to air the year's grievances and welcome the new year together. It works as a social cleanser.
abissa.meaning: It shows that Akan kingship is still alive: king, queen mother and rituals coexist within the modern state.
abissa.use: Go to Grand-Bassam from late October to early November to see it. Ask before taking photos and respect sacred moments; explain the idea of forgiveness and criticism to guests first so they understand what they see.
abissa.bridge: Like the 'world turned upside down' of European carnival, or the way temple festivals in Taiwan bind a community together.
abissa.where: Public squares in Quartier France, Grand-Bassam.

baoule.name: Masques et statues baoulé
baoule.signal: A long, slender carved face with a calm expression and lowered eyelids, the hair and facial marks carved in fine detail; or a seated pair of male and female figures.
baoule.what: The Baoulé, part of the Akan world, are known for realistic, elegant portrait masks (used in Mblo performances) and 'other-world spouse' figures (blolo bian / blolo bla). Baoulé people believe everyone has a spouse in the other world (blolo); when life goes badly, a diviner may say that spouse is jealous, and a beautiful figure is carved for it and cared for.
baoule.why: In Baoulé aesthetics, calm, symmetry and refinement stand for moral goodness and beauty; portrait masks are sometimes carved after a real person.
baoule.meaning: West African masks were a major inspiration for early 20th-century European modern art. Today they live on in contemporary design, such as Loza Maléombho's gold mask clasps.
baoule.use: When buying a mask, ask about its origin: most on the market are decorative pieces made for tourists, and antiques need provenance and an export permit. Asking is itself a sign of taste.
baoule.bridge: Compare Japanese Noh masks: both are ritual masks that later entered museums and the collectors' market, and both find beauty in stillness.
baoule.where: Museum of Civilisations; around Bouaké and Sakassou in the centre.

goldweights.signal: In museums or antique shops, boxes of thumb-sized brass figures: crocodiles, birds, old men, geometric shapes, each a different weight.
goldweights.what: The Akan world used gold dust as currency, and these lost-wax brass weights were used to weigh it. Many shapes correspond to a proverb.
goldweights.why: Gold was the foundation of Akan kingship. The weights were both business tools and 'proverbs you can hold', so every transaction was also an exchange of wisdom.
goldweights.meaning: They bring together Akan commerce, metalwork and oral wisdom, and explain the saying that to speak of the king is to speak of gold.
goldweights.use: A small weight makes a great gift and conversation piece. Ask 'Which proverb does this shape stand for?' to open a rich conversation. Again, know the difference between new pieces and antiques.
goldweights.bridge: Compare the Chinese abacus and inscribed seals, or Japanese netsuke: small objects holding big culture.
goldweights.where: Museum of Civilisations; reputable antique dealers.

kita.signal: A thick cloth pieced together from strips a dozen or so centimetres wide, geometric patterns alternating square by square, worn over the shoulders of elders at weddings.
kita.what: Côte d'Ivoire's traditional hand-woven cloth, for which the Baoulé of the centre and the Yacouba around Man in the west are both known. In 2023 Ivorian traditional weaving was inscribed as UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage.
kita.why: A narrow loom can only weave narrow strips, so the cloth is 'pieced' together. A good cloth takes a long time to weave, so it became a symbol of wealth and family status.
kita.meaning: Worn on important occasions such as weddings and the Dot (bride-price ceremony), it is a language of status, family and respect, far above printed cloth in price and standing.
kita.use: Telling printed wax from hand-woven Kita separates the outsider from the insider: on hand-woven cloth, look for the seams between strips.
kita.bridge: Compare Ghana's Kente (from the same Akan world) and Japan's Nishijin weaving: ceremonial high-end textiles.
kita.where: Weaving villages around Tiébissou; craftspeople in the Man region.

wax.signal: Bright printed cotton everywhere, with brand names printed along the selvedge; at big events whole streets wear the same pattern.
wax.what: The most important cloth in West African daily and ceremonial life. Abidjan's Uniwax is the leading factory, and it issues commemorative designs for major events, such as the 50th anniversary of independence, the 2023 Africa Cup of Nations and the national team's champions' cloth.
wax.why: Wax began in the 19th century as Dutch industrial imitations of Indonesian batik. They sold poorly in Indonesia, were sold in West Africa instead, and became 'African cloth'. Patterns have names and stories, so the cloth itself is a language.
wax.meaning: From national events to family weddings and funerals, wearing the same cloth signals belonging and support.
wax.use: The story that 'African cloth actually comes from Indonesia' works every time with Asian guests. When invited to a wedding, first ask whether the hosts have chosen a 'uniforme' cloth.
wax.bridge: A direct link to Indonesian batik: one cloth ties together the trade history of Asia, Europe and Africa.
wax.where: Major markets and Uniwax shops; have a tailor make it to measure.

senufo.nameZh: Senufo: painted cloth, hornbill figures and the Poro society
senufo.signal: Coarse cotton painted with natural dyes in silhouettes of birds, fish and masked dancers; a carved wooden hornbill with a long beak, a big belly and spread wings.
senufo.what: The Senufo are the main people of the northern Gur world, centred on Korhogo. Their painted cloth (toiles de Korhogo), hornbill figures and masks are often linked to the Poro society, a secret society responsible for male initiation and traditional education.
senufo.why: In the Senufo cosmology the hornbill is one of the first creatures, a symbol of fertility and knowledge. Many motifs on the painted cloth come from ritual and myth.
senufo.meaning: Senufo carving is among the Ivorian art most often seen in Western museums, and painted cloth is the north's most portable cultural ambassador.
senufo.use: Seeing a hornbill and saying 'that's Senufo, from the north' sets it apart from southern Baoulé style. But do not ask about Poro's secret rituals.
senufo.bridge: Compare Mali's bogolan mud cloth and Japanese indigo dyeing; the secret society can be compared with initiation systems elsewhere.
senufo.where: Workshops in Korhogo in the north; craft markets in Abidjan.

dan.name: Masques dan · échassiers de Man
dan.nameZh: The mask world of the Dan / Yacouba
dan.signal: A dark, glossy wooden mask with round or slit eyes; in the western mountains, dancers on stilts two or three metres high spinning in the air.
dan.what: The Dan (also called Yacouba) are a Mandé people of the mountains around Man in the west. Their masks are seen as embodiments of forest spirits, each with a role: justice, entertainment, carrying messages. The stilt dance is one of the west's most famous performances.
dan.why: In this world a mask is not decoration but a living presence; the person wearing it is the spirit itself.
dan.meaning: The western mountains, with waterfalls, liana bridges and peaks, are among the country's most beautiful landscapes, and the region where mask culture is best preserved.
dan.use: When locals say 'the mask is out', understand that it does not mean 'someone is wearing a mask' but that a sacred moment has begun. Speak respectfully and ask before taking photos.
dan.bridge: Compare Japanese kagura: once the dancer puts on the mask, in the ritual he is seen as the deity itself, not someone playing it.
dan.where: Man and surrounding villages in the west; easiest to see at festivals.

zaouli.signal: A dancer in a brightly coloured mask and raffia skirt, the upper body almost still, the feet moving too fast to follow.
zaouli.what: The mask dance of the Gouro people, inscribed as UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2017.
zaouli.why: The Gouro belong to the southern Mandé and live west of the Baoulé; their masks combine animal and human features, and the rhythm comes from drums and flutes.
zaouli.meaning: One of the country's most visually striking traditional performances, often representing Côte d'Ivoire at national ceremonies.
zaouli.use: See it live once and you will understand why people say the feet move too fast to see.
zaouli.bridge: Compare Taiwan's temple procession troupes, such as the Ba Jia Jiang: demanding physical performance at local festivals, carrying faith and community identity.
zaouli.where: Festivals around Bouaflé and Zuénoula; festivals such as MASA.

patheo.signal: African political and business leaders at formal events in wide, long-sleeved shirts pieced from printed cloth, instead of suits.
patheo.what: Born Pathé Ouédraogo in Burkina Faso in 1950, he came to Abidjan in the 1970s and grew from a street tailor into a brand with shops in about ten African countries, known for its printed-cloth shirts (chemise pagne).
patheo.why: In 1993 the singer Miriam Makeba bought five of his shirts in Abidjan as a gift for Nelson Mandela. Mandela later wore them on the international stage, giving 'formal wear in African cloth' political standing. The King of Morocco and Rwanda's President Kagame have also worn his designs.
patheo.meaning: He represents the confidence of 'Africans designing formal wear for Africans'; a new generation of Ivorian designers, such as Gilles Touré, call him their mentor.
patheo.use: For an occasion that calls for something formal with an African touch, a Pathé'O shirt is the safest choice. Tell the Mandela and Makeba story and people will know you have done your homework.
patheo.bridge: Like the Mao suit or the Tang jacket for Chinese leaders: a garment that is a political and cultural statement.
patheo.where: His workshop and shop in Treichville.

loza.signal: A sharp jacket fastened with a gold Baoulé mask clasp, from a collection called 'Zaouli'.
loza.what: An Ivorian-American designer who founded her label in New York in 2009 and moved back to Abidjan in 2012 to start again. Beyoncé wore one of her jackets in the 2020 video for 'Already', and her work is in the collection of the V&A in London.
loza.why: She felt African symbols, textiles and aesthetics were absent from international fashion, so she chose to stay in Abidjan and redesign from traditional symbols.
loza.meaning: She proves you can become globally known without leaving Abidjan, a benchmark for a new generation of Ivorian creatives.
loza.use: Anyone can talk about Beyoncé; it is more tasteful to talk about how the mask clasp turns a ritual object into an everyday accessory.
loza.bridge: Compare Asian designers who turn traditional motifs into high fashion: using tradition to speak about the present.

zouglou.signal: In a maquis the whole room sings along to a song with funny lyrics; at weddings people dripping in gold dance and throw money.
zouglou.what: Zouglou emerged in 1990 among university residences in Yopougon, Abidjan, singing about daily life with humour and self-mockery. Coupé-décalé is party dance music started in the early 2000s by the Ivorian diaspora in Paris, often with displays of wealth and money-throwing. In Nouchi, the 'gaou' of 'Premier Gaou' means a fool or a newbie.
zouglou.why: Zouglou was born in a time of student protest and economic slump, a way of laughing through hardship; Coupé-décalé was born in the crisis years, fighting heaviness with lightness and show.
zouglou.meaning: They are the sound of Abidjan. Magic System's 'Premier Gaou' (2000) was a hit across the French-speaking world and carried Ivorian pop culture worldwide.
zouglou.use: Humming 'Premier Gaou' brings people closer instantly. Moving a little when Coupé-décalé comes on in a maquis works better than anything else.
zouglou.bridge: Zouglou is like Taiwanese-language pop: everyday language about everyday life, with self-mockery and warmth.

alpha.signal: Older taxi drivers listening to reggae with lyrics mixing French, English and Dioula, about peace, corruption and African unity.
alpha.what: Born in Dimbokro in the centre in 1953, one of Africa's best-known reggae singers, known for 'Brigadier Sabari' and 'Jerusalem'.
alpha.why: Reggae became a vehicle for political commentary in West Africa. His breakthrough song 'Brigadier Sabari' is about being beaten during a police street sweep in Abidjan, considered the first time a West African singer openly sang about police violence; he went on to criticise corruption and civil war in song.
alpha.meaning: He made Côte d'Ivoire 'Africa's reggae capital', and kept calling for peace through the crisis years.
alpha.use: Talking about him with locals over 40 is talking about their youth.
alpha.bridge: Like Lo Ta-yu in Taiwan: a pop musician who is also a social commentator.
alpha.where: His concerts; reggae bars in Abidjan.

drogba.name: Les Éléphants · Didier Drogba
drogba.nameZh: The national team 'The Elephants' and Drogba
drogba.signal: On match days the whole city wears orange, white and green; fans tell you, quite seriously, that a player once helped halt a civil war with a television appeal.
drogba.what: On 8 October 2005, after the national team qualified for the World Cup, captain Drogba knelt with his teammates in the dressing room and, on live television, called on both sides of the civil war to lay down their arms; days later the sides agreed to a ceasefire. Côte d'Ivoire won the 2015 Africa Cup of Nations and, as hosts, won the 2023 edition in early 2024.
drogba.why: In a country divided by politics and ethnicity, the national team is one of the few moments when everyone is on the same side.
drogba.meaning: Football binds national identity; the 2024 title was seen as a symbol of national revival.
drogba.use: A safe topic with anyone. Knowing about the 2005 appeal lets you move from football to the country's history without touching political positions.
drogba.bridge: Like baseball in Taiwan: national team games create a shared feeling beyond political divides.

kourouma.signal: On the bookshelves of Abidjan's elite, a book called The Suns of Independence; the full name of the national cultural palace in Treichville is 'Palais de la Culture Bernard Binlin-Dadié'.
kourouma.what: Ahmadou Kourouma (1927–2003) wrote Les Soleils des indépendances (1968, first published in Montreal) about disillusion after independence, and Allah n'est pas obligé (2000, Prix Renaudot) about child soldiers. Bernard Dadié (1916–2019), born in Assinie, was a writer and playwright and minister of culture from 1977 to 1986, known as the 'father of Ivorian literature', author of Climbié and Un Nègre à Paris.
kourouma.why: Kourouma brought the rhythm and thought of Malinké into French and changed African literature in French; Dadié, through his long life and work, witnessed a whole century from colonisation to independence.
kourouma.meaning: Literature conveys the hopes and disappointments after independence with more warmth than history books.
kourouma.use: Mentioning that you are reading Kourouma at an elite dinner is a powerful cultural signal. Allah n'est pas obligé is available in English as Allah Is Not Obliged.
kourouma.bridge: Compare Pai Hsien-yung or Huang Chun-ming: a society's transformation told through ordinary people.
kourouma.where: Bookshops in Abidjan (such as Librairie de France); second-hand bookshops in France.

chocolatier.signal: A row of handmade chocolate bars in wrappers printed with African cloth patterns, labelled with the cocoa region 'Daloa'.
chocolatier.what: A chocolate brand founded by former banker Axel Emmanuel Gbaou, who buys beans from local cooperatives and makes chocolate in his Cocody workshop; it won an award at the Paris agricultural show in 2022.
chocolatier.why: The world's largest cocoa producer long had almost no local premium chocolate. He represents a new generation keeping 'bean to bar' at home.
chocolatier.meaning: A symbol of cocoa moving from raw material to brand, supported by the Coffee and Cocoa Council and promoted abroad.
chocolatier.use: The best gift for Asian guests. Say one line: 'Most of the world's chocolate starts here, but local fine chocolate is only just beginning.'
chocolatier.bridge: Compare Japan's artisan chocolate culture, and Taiwan's specialty coffee going from farm to brand.
chocolatier.where: Workshop and shop in Cocody; some supermarkets.

maquis.nameZh: Open-air restaurants and attiéké with grilled fish
maquis.signal: Plastic chairs by the road at night, charcoal and whole grilled fish with a plate of off-white, slightly sour grains, and Coupé-décalé blasting from the speakers.
maquis.what: A maquis is an Ivorian open-air restaurant whose signature is grilled fish or chicken with attiéké (fermented cassava grains), chilli sauce and raw onion and tomato. The street version, fried tuna with attiéké, is called garba. In December 2024 the know-how of making attiéké was inscribed as UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage.
maquis.why: Attiéké is a tradition of the southern lagoon peoples, made and sold mostly by women; 'maquis' originally meant 'bush' and came to mean a people's restaurant.
maquis.meaning: The maquis is the centre of Abidjan's social life, where bosses, officials and students all sit. Knowing maquis says more about being a local than knowing five-star restaurants.
maquis.use: A good maquis meal often stays with Asian guests longer than a fine restaurant. Eat with your right hand and order a local beer.
maquis.bridge: Like Taiwan's re-chao stir-fry restaurants or a Japanese izakaya: real socialising happens here, not in formal restaurants.
maquis.where: Famous places in Yopougon, Marcory and Cocody; ask a local friend to take you to their regular spot.

kedjenou.nameZh: Three keywords of Ivorian home cooking
kedjenou.signal: A sealed clay pot brought to the table holding chicken and vegetables stewed into a rich broth; a sticky yellow or white ball of foutou with red palm-nut sauce; plantains frying in a roadside pan.
kedjenou.what: Kedjenou is chicken slow-cooked with almost no water in a sealed clay pot (canari), shaken from time to time as it cooks; the name is said to come from the Baoulé word for shaking. Foutou is plantain or yam pounded into a ball, served with sauce graine (palm-nut sauce) or sauce arachide (peanut sauce). Alloco is fried plantain, often with chilli sauce and grilled fish.
kedjenou.why: These foods match different cultural worlds: plantain, yam and palm nuts from the southern forest, grains and peanuts from the northern savannah. Kedjenou is generally thought to come from the Baoulé of the centre.
kedjenou.meaning: Eating the right dish in the right way is a sign of respect for your host's culture.
kedjenou.use: When invited to a home, ask 'Which region is this recipe from?' and hosts are usually happy to tell. Pinch off a small piece of foutou with your right hand and dip it in the sauce.
kedjenou.bridge: Compare Asian clay-pot stews and pounded rice cakes such as mochi: the same pairing of a slow-cooked pot and a pounded staple.

bangui.nameZh: Palm wine, ginger juice and hibiscus tea
bangui.signal: Milky, slightly fizzy drinks sold by the roadside; fiery ginger juice in plastic bags; deep-red iced hibiscus tea.
bangui.what: Bangui is palm wine, naturally fermented from palm sap and often called the national drink; gnamakoudji is fresh ginger juice; bissap is hibiscus tea. The last two are the most common soft drinks. Distilled palm wine becomes the spirit koutoukou.
bangui.why: Palm wine matters in southern rituals: at weddings, funerals and reconciliations it is often first poured on the ground for the ancestors, then shared. Ginger juice and hibiscus tea are everyday drinks across West Africa.
bangui.meaning: What you drink is a social language: bangui means closeness to the village and tradition; imported champagne means showing off.
bangui.use: For guests who do not drink alcohol, a gnamakoudji or bissap is both local and thoughtful. Before drinking bangui, your host may pour a little on the ground for the ancestors (a libation); do not laugh, just wait quietly.
bangui.bridge: Compare millet wine in Taiwanese Indigenous rituals.

assinie.signal: On Friday afternoons, Abidjan's luxury cars head east; the Atlantic on one side, the lagoon on the other, villas and resorts in between.
assinie.what: A narrow peninsula about 90 km east of Abidjan between the Atlantic and the Aby Lagoon, the weekend retreat of Abidjan's elite and expatriates. The point where the lagoon meets the sea is called La Passe.
assinie.why: Abidjan's own beaches have big waves and are poor for swimming, while Assinie's lagoon side is calm and private.
assinie.meaning: 'The weekend in Assinie' marks upper-class life in Abidjan, and is a place for informal socialising and business. It is also the birthplace of the writer Bernard Dadié, and where French missionaries and traders first settled in the late 17th century.
assinie.use: Being invited to a villa in Assinie for the weekend signals that you are 'inside the circle'. Bring an interesting gift, Taiwanese tea for example.
assinie.bridge: Like Kenting for Taipei, or Hayama and Karuizawa for Tokyo: a wealthy weekend not far from the city.

parks.signal: In the south-western rainforest, chimpanzees crack nuts with stones; in the north-eastern savannah, rivers wind through wide open grassland.
parks.what: Taï National Park (UNESCO, 1982) is one of the last large tracts of primary rainforest in West Africa; its chimpanzees choose stones as hammers and anvils to crack nuts, a classic site for studying tool use in animals. Comoé National Park (inscribed 1983), about 11,500 km², is West Africa's largest national park; it was placed on the List of World Heritage in Danger after the civil war and removed in 2017.
parks.why: Côte d'Ivoire's forest cover has shrunk sharply because of cocoa farming, and these two parks are its last ecological treasures.
parks.meaning: They are the counterpoint in the cocoa-and-forest debate, and hold potential for eco-tourism.
parks.use: With guests who care about sustainability, talk about Taï's chimpanzee research and cocoa's toll on the forest. Guided visits must be arranged in advance.
parks.bridge: Like Taroko or Yushan in Taiwan: the nation's natural calling cards.
parks.where: South-west (Taï), north-east (Comoé); both need advance arrangements.

b01.name: The Four Cultural Worlds
b01.nameZh: How 60-plus ethnic groups fall into four families
b01.signal: In one country, masks from the south are finely realistic, carvings from the north are abstract and powerful, and masks from the west are dark and mysterious. One person is called Ouattara, another Kouassi, another Gbagbo.
b01.what: Côte d'Ivoire has more than 60 ethnic groups, which scholars usually group into four cultural worlds: the Akan of the south-east and centre (Baoulé, Agni, N'zima and others), the Kru of the south-west (Bété, Dida, Wè and others), the Mandé of the north and west (Malinké/Dioula in the north; Dan/Yacouba and Gouro in the west), and the Gur or Voltaic peoples of the north (Senufo, Lobi, Koulango).
b01.why: The borders were drawn by colonisers, but the peoples cross them: the Akan extend into Ghana, the Mandé into Mali and Guinea, the Senufo into Burkina Faso and Mali. To understand an object, first ask which cultural world it belongs to, not whether it is 'Ivorian'.
b01.meaning: This map is the starting point for reading everything else. Masks, cloth, music, festivals, surnames and even the political map can first be placed in one of these four worlds.
b01.use: A name often hints at where someone comes from. Day names such as Kouassi, Kouadio or Yao usually come from the Akan; Ouattara, Coulibaly, Traoré and Diabaté usually from the Mandé/Dioula north. Bring it up lightly, out of curiosity, and never use it as a label.
b01.bridge: Like Taiwan's Hoklo, Hakka, post-1949 and Indigenous communities: one country, several languages, cuisines and rituals, each connected across the sea or a border to somewhere else.

b02.name: The Legend of Abla Pokou
b02.nameZh: Queen Pokou and the birth of the Baoulé
b02.signal: When Ivorians tell the story of the time before the nation, they almost always mention a queen who sacrificed her own son for her people. The name Baoulé is said to come from that moment.
b02.what: According to legend, in the 18th century a branch of the Akan left present-day Ghana after a succession dispute, led westward by Queen Abla Pokou. Trapped against the Comoé River by pursuers, she offered her son to the river spirit, and her people crossed to safety. 'Ba-ou-li' is said to mean 'the child is dead', and from then on the group was called Baoulé.
b02.why: It is the founding myth of the Baoulé, and it explains why people in central Côte d'Ivoire are so close to Ghana's Ashanti in language, kingship and gold culture.
b02.meaning: The Baoulé are among the country's largest groups, and the first president, Houphouët-Boigny, was Baoulé. The story is part of the national narrative, retold in schoolbooks, theatre and novels.
b02.use: Mention Abla Pokou to a Baoulé friend and they will be surprised you know it. Tell it with respect: it is a sacred origin story, not a curiosity.
b02.bridge: A 'migration and sacrifice' founding myth, comparable to founding legends in many cultures: one person's sacrifice gives birth to a whole people.

b03.name: The Kong Empire and the Dioula Trade Network
b03.nameZh: Northern trade routes, Islam and mud-brick mosques
b03.signal: Northern towns have mud-brick mosques bristling with wooden stakes; many traders in the markets speak Dioula; Ouattara is a common surname in the north.
b03.what: In the early 18th century the Ouattara family founded the state of Kong in the north, a hub for the trade in kola nuts, gold, cloth and salt. Mandé-speaking Dioula merchants, travelling the routes from the Niger River to the forest, carried Islam and Sudanese-style mud architecture southward. Kong was destroyed by Samory Touré in 1897.
b03.why: The north was never a 'periphery'. It was the southern end of the trans-Saharan network: kola nuts went north from the southern forests, while salt, cloth and Islamic learning came south.
b03.meaning: In 2021 eight Sudanese-style mosques in the north were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List, a sign of the blending of Senufo and Malinké cultures. Dioula is still the common language of trade in markets across the country.
b03.use: In the north or among Dioula traders, talking about Kong and the mud-brick mosques builds more rapport than talking about Abidjan. Kola nuts are still a common gift when visiting elders.
b03.bridge: Like the southern terminus of the Silk Roads: merchants brought religion, architecture and language along with their goods.

b04.name: The Story of Four Capitals
b04.signal: The official capital is Yamoussoukro, yet the presidency, ministries, embassies and company headquarters are almost all in Abidjan; Grand-Bassam and Bingerville still hold fading colonial buildings.
b04.what: Under French rule the capital was first Grand-Bassam (1893). After yellow fever struck it moved to higher ground at Bingerville (1900), then in 1934 to Abidjan, which had a port. In 1983 Houphouët-Boigny made his home town Yamoussoukro the official capital, but the real political and economic centre stayed in Abidjan.
b04.why: Each move reflected the priority of its time: first coastal trade, then public health, then a deep-water port and railway, and finally political symbolism and the president's birthplace.
b04.meaning: A trip through Grand-Bassam, Bingerville, Abidjan and Yamoussoukro is modern history in miniature.
b04.use: When you take guests to Grand-Bassam or Bingerville, tie it together in one line: 'This used to be the capital, until…'. The visit instantly feels deeper.
b04.bridge: Like Taiwan's political centre moving from Tainan to Taipei, or purpose-built capitals such as Brasília and Naypyidaw.

b05.name: Houphouët-Boigny and the 'Ivorian Miracle'
b05.nameZh: The founding father, cocoa and modernist confidence
b05.signal: Abidjan's Plateau district has a run of bold 1960s–70s modern buildings: La Pyramide, Hôtel Ivoire, towers on the lagoon. Many institutions, bridges and universities are named after Félix Houphouët-Boigny.
b05.what: Félix Houphouët-Boigny, a Baoulé cocoa planter, doctor and politician, was president from independence in 1960 until his death in 1993. Coffee and cocoa exports and close ties with France brought strong growth in the 1960s and 70s, known as the 'Ivorian miracle', and Abidjan was nicknamed 'the Manhattan of Africa'.
b05.why: When cocoa prices collapsed in the 1980s a debt crisis followed and the miracle faded. But the buildings, hotels and urban scale of that era still form Abidjan's skeleton.
b05.meaning: Most of the 'grand' buildings you see in Abidjan are products of that optimistic era. Once you know this, you can read the city's confidence and its sense of loss.
b05.use: Point at La Pyramide or Hôtel Ivoire and say: 'This is architecture from the Ivorian miracle.' Then add that Abidjan once had an ice rink and an international conference centre. It is the most effective way to open a city tour.
b05.bridge: Like Taiwan's economic miracle and its Ten Major Construction Projects, or Singapore's founding story: a strong leader, a period of high growth and a set of symbolic buildings.

b06.name: The Cocoa Economy
b06.signal: On the roads west and into the centre, cocoa beans dry by the roadside and trucks pass loaded with sacks, yet supermarkets carry few local premium chocolate brands.
b06.what: Côte d'Ivoire is the world's largest cocoa producer, grown mostly by hundreds of thousands of smallholders in the forest zone. The state sets the farm-gate price through the Coffee and Cocoa Council (CCC). For decades most beans have been exported to Europe for processing.
b06.why: Cocoa fuelled the Ivorian miracle and also lit the fuse of crisis: when world prices move, the nation's finances and politics move with them.
b06.meaning: Cocoa shapes public finances, rural life and migration (many farm workers come from Burkina Faso and Mali), and is tied to international issues such as child labour and deforestation. Making chocolate locally is now seen as a symbol of moving up the value chain.
b06.use: Cocoa prices and local processing are a safe and substantial topic with business people. A gift of local handmade chocolate for Asian guests is the perfect way to tell this story.
b06.bridge: Like sugar in Taiwan's past, or coffee in Ethiopia: one crop shaping a whole country's economy and society.

b07.name: The Crisis Years
b07.nameZh: From the 'Ivoirité' debate to reconciliation in 2011
b07.signal: People over 40 often refer to 'la crise'; some artworks are full of war imagery; at dinners, everyone quietly avoids certain political subjects.
b07.what: After Houphouët-Boigny died in 1993, the 'ivoirité' debate over who counted as a 'true Ivorian' intensified. Civil war broke out in 2002 and the country was split north and south for years; a post-election crisis followed in 2010–2011. Since 2011 the country has entered a period of reconstruction and high growth.
b07.why: Overlapping questions of ethnicity, religion, land and migration, together with the distribution of cocoa wealth, made political divisions especially sharp.
b07.meaning: This period shaped a generation's memory and inspired much art (Aboudia, for example). Hosting the 2024 Africa Cup of Nations was widely seen as a sign that the country was back on its feet.
b07.use: Treat it as background for understanding, not a topic to raise. If someone brings it up, listen and do not take sides. In art circles, how works respond to the crisis is a safe and thoughtful way in.
b07.bridge: Comparable to any society that has been through division and transitional justice: the memories are still fresh, and everyone has learned which things are better left unsaid.

b08.name: Nouchi
b08.signal: Suddenly you cannot follow young people's French: 'On dit quoi?', 'Y'a pas drap', 'C'est comment?'. The same mixed phrases appear on billboards.
b08.what: Nouchi is a mixed language that emerged among Abidjan's street youth in the 1970s and 80s. It is built on French, with words from Dioula, Baoulé, Bété and other languages, and from English.
b08.why: In a city of more than 60 ethnic groups, young people needed an urban common tongue that belonged to no single group.
b08.meaning: Nouchi has moved from fringe slang to part of national identity. It runs through Zouglou, Coupé-décalé and advertising, and it marks someone as an Abidjanais.
b08.use: A few words of Nouchi can warm up a conversation in a maquis or a taxi instantly. Do not use it in formal settings, and do not overdo it to the point of mimicry.
b08.bridge: Like Taiwanese-accented Mandarin or Hong Kong's mix of Cantonese and English: it expresses a city identity, not just a way of speaking.

b09.name: France's Shadow and a Diverse Business Scene
b09.nameZh: The CFA franc, French schooling and Lebanese traders
b09.signal: Money is the West African CFA franc (XOF); the elite speak with a Parisian accent and holiday in France; many supermarkets, hardware stores and restaurants are run by Lebanese families; Chinese signs appear more and more on new building sites.
b09.what: Since independence, Côte d'Ivoire has kept close ties with France in currency, education, defence and business. The Lebanese community has traded here since the early 20th century and still controls much of retail and wholesale; in recent years Chinese, Indian, Turkish and Moroccan capital has become increasingly active.
b09.why: The colonial legacy and a pro-French path after independence carried French influence into daily life, while an open trading economy drew wave after wave of foreign merchants.
b09.meaning: Knowing who does which business lets you read Abidjan's commercial map, and shows what role you can play as an Asian.
b09.use: Working with Lebanese-owned businesses is often the fastest route into business in Abidjan. At elite dinners, French culture (literature, wine, Paris) is the shared language.
b09.bridge: Like Hong Kong and Britain, or Singapore's diverse business scene: colonial language and institutions, plus trading networks divided along ethnic lines.

b10.name: The Religious Map
b10.nameZh: A Muslim north, a Christian south, and living traditions
b10.signal: Dawn in the north brings the call to prayer; churches in the south are full on Sundays; Harrist believers in white gather by the sea; many Christian families still honour their ancestors.
b10.what: Islam predominates in the north, and Catholicism, Protestantism and evangelical churches in the south, alongside home-grown faiths such as the Harrist Church, which grew from the prophet William Wadé Harris's coastal preaching in the 1910s. Traditional beliefs and ancestral rites coexist with all of them.
b10.why: Islam arrived along the northern trade routes, Christianity landed on the coast with colonisation and mission schools, and the two met in the centre.
b10.meaning: Most of the time faiths coexist peacefully; interfaith marriages and visits during each other's festivals are common. Yet in times of political mobilisation, religion has also been used as a dividing line.
b10.use: Adjust invitations during Ramadan, dress more conservatively when visiting the north, and at the Yamoussoukro basilica talk about architecture rather than faith. All of this is part of good taste.
b10.bridge: Like religious life in Taiwan: Buddhism, Taoism, folk religion and Christianity side by side, often blended in daily practice.

b11.name: The Festival Calendar
b11.era: Chapter 11 · The rhythm of the year
b11.signal: Sometimes the whole city suddenly empties (everyone has gone home for Paquinou or the yam festival); sometimes the streets fill with drums and processions (Abissa in Grand-Bassam).
b11.what: A rough calendar: in March–April, the Dipri festival (Gomon), Paquinou (the Baoulé Easter homecoming), FEMUA, Abidjan Art Week and MASA (even years); August–October is yam-festival season; late October to early November is Abissa in Grand-Bassam; November–December brings the Dakar Biennale (Dak'Art, 19 November–19 December 2026).
b11.why: Traditional festivals follow the farming calendar (the yam harvest, for example), while modern arts events are mostly held in the dry season, when they are easier to run.
b11.meaning: Festivals display identity and social ties: who comes home, who pays, and who sits next to the king all send messages.
b11.use: Check this calendar before planning a guest's trip. Taking guests to the right festival at the right time is hospitality at its finest.
b11.bridge: Like Taiwan's Mazu pilgrimage or Japan's matsuri: religion, community and tourism woven together.

b12.name: Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana
b12.nameZh: One Akan world, two colonial fates
b12.signal: Kita cloth looks very like Kente; Baoulé and Ashanti gold jewellery speak the same language; yet one country speaks French and the other English, and they joke about which is better.
b12.what: Akan culture spans the border. Ghana was a British colony and became independent in 1957; Côte d'Ivoire was French and became independent in 1960. They are the world's first and second largest cocoa producers, together about 60 per cent of global output.
b12.why: A colonial border cut one cultural world in two, and the two countries then took different paths in language, law and politics.
b12.meaning: Each is the other's most important reference point: they coordinate cocoa policy and are both rivals and siblings culturally.
b12.use: Being able to explain how Kita relates to Kente, and Baoulé to Ashanti, marks you in both countries as someone who 'really knows West Africa'.
b12.bridge: Like Malaysia and Indonesia, both part of the Malay world: one cultural base split by British and Dutch colonisers, each with its own official language and path, yet still sharing food, dress and royal traditions.
